 Alaska’s Senate race could be decided by ranked-choice voting. Here’s how that works 
 By Jim Saksa 
 November 16, 2026 
 Prefer us on Google 
 to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Bluesky 
 The last uncalled Senate race of the 2026 midterms is befittingly playing out in the “Last Frontier”: Alaska. And the winners of that contest and the race for Alaska’s single U.S. House seat could be decided by the state’s ranked-choice voting (RCV) system.  
 Confused about that? You’re not alone.
 RCV has grown in popularity in recent years as jurisdictions across the country have adopted it. But each system has its own quirks. Here’s how it works in Alaska.
 Four candidates, no majority?
 As of Monday morning, Alaska has counted 97% of the vote. In the extremely close Senate race, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) with 49.9% to his 46%. 
 In the House race , Republican Rep. Nick Begich III has 47.7% of the vote, followed by independent Bill Hill with 41.7%, Democrat Eric Hafner with 7.8% and Libertarian Jim McDermott with 2.6%. (Democratic officials urged voters to support Hill over Hafner , who made the ballot even though he’s a federal prison inmate with no record of ever living in Alaska.)
 In both races, ranked-choice voting will kick if no candidate clears 50% of the vote by Wednesday’s ballot count deadline. 
 In Alaska, primaries are nonpartisan, meaning voters of all party affiliations use the same ballot and the top four candidates with the most votes all advance to the general election.

 It also means you can see multiple candidates from the same party facing off in November — this year , Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the governorship against three Republican candidates. 
 That’s why, besides Peltola, the Senate race features three Republican candidates: Sen. Sullivan, Gerald L. Heikes and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is listed on the ballot without a party affiliation. 
 In the general election, voters can rank up to all four candidates in order of preference, but they don’t have to — someone committed to just one candidate could vote for only him and leave the second, third and fourth choices blank. Alaska initially counts everyone’s first-choice vote, and if no candidate wins a majority there, then election officials turn to RCV tabulation to determine a winner. 
 At that point, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their votes are reallocated to other candidates based on who Alaskans picked as their second choice. If a voter only ranks eliminated candidates, their votes remain with them — there is no reallocation. 
 If still no candidate clears 50% after the first reallocation round, the process repeats itself again, with the third-place candidate’s votes redistributed to voters’ second, third or fourth choice (if their higher-ranked choices were already eliminated).
 Alaska adopted RCV in 2020 and implemented it in 2022. Voters there have twice rejected GOP-led attempts to repeal it, including a ballot measure this year. 
 RCV critics sometimes unfairly blame it for Alaska’s slow vote count , but the real culprit is the state’s massive size, harsh winter weather and a number of communities accessible only by plane or boat. The state also has not adopted electronic poll books, which slows the processing of the vote count considerably. 
 To accommodate for those delays, Alaska law gives absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day a 10-day grace period to arrive and be counted (and a 15-day period for overseas voters). 
 During that 15-day period, the Alaska Division of Elections only reports first-choice results. Only once that window closes does the RCV tabulation occur. The RCV tally process itself only takes a few minutes. 
 The reason why both of Alaska’s congressional races have yet to be called is due to the state’s decision to not release preliminary RCV results, unlike most other jurisdictions using RCV. 
 On Saturday, NBC News reported that Peltola is on track to win the Alaska Senate race regardless of whether she secures a first-round majority of the vote or it heads into RCV tabulation.
 Incoming challenge?
 Regardless of when the vote count is complete and the winner is declared, it probably won’t be the end of the story. Republicans appear poised to challenge the results.
 They currently allege that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a little-known retired teacher, is a Democratic plant intended to siphon off votes from incumbent Sen. Sullivan. 
 President Donald Trump even ordered the Department of Justice (DOJ) to sue Alaska ahead of Election Day to block certification of the results unless Sen. Sullivan won. 
 After a federal judge quickly dismissed the suit, the DOJ immediately appealed.* But the status of that appeal remains uncertain as the government has not yet filed a brief in support.
 On Monday morning, Trump posted a video on social media that asserted Democrats had cheated in Alaska, escalating a string of threats his administration has made against the state.
 *The Elias Law Group (ELG) represents the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in this case. ELG Firm Chair Marc Elias is the founder of Democracy Docket.
